# Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable

Marius De Kuthy Meurers Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Aaron Parisi
Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Bernd Bohnet Corresponding author:
mdkm@google.com, aarontp@google.com, bohnetbd@google.com Affiliation:
Google DeepMind

###### Abstract

LLMs are increasingly consulted for moral judgment. We aim to improve
performance on such tasks by rewarding good arguments, on the premise
that arguing well increases the likelihood of judging well. We train a
reinforcement learning policy initialized from a state-of-the-art
language model in a self-judged tournament with masked thinking: the
generated arguments are judged pairwise on argument quality by the
policy itself. As an empirical basis, we extract authentic dilemmas from
classic novels, using a logic solver to verify that each constitutes a
conflict. We show that our judge rates argument quality like human
annotators, and the policy then adopts the language register that it
rewards. Testing on the external benchmarks MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and
MORABLES, we find that the policy becomes more decisive and invariant to
the order in which options are presented, but sycophancy and reframing
remain a challenge to validity. Two ablation studies with synthetic
dilemmas and unmasked thinking match the reordering gains, but show a
weaker register shift and higher sycophancy. We conclude that
consistency is not validity: consistency under reordering can be
optimized without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal.

###### keywords

reinforcement learning, argument quality, moral judgment, sycophancy,
LLM-as-a-judge

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for moral
judgment ([Cheng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)), yet machine ethics
research predominantly treats moral reasoning as discrete label
prediction ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib28); [Marraffini et al.,
2024](#bib.bib42)). However, genuine moral decisions require
argumentation involving weighing conflicting duties, comparing
consequences, and justifying trade-offs ([Talat et al.,
2022](#bib.bib57); [Hancox-Li and Blili-Hamelin, 2024](#bib.bib27)).
Models trained only on final decisions tend to produce brittle judgments
([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib36); [An and Du, 2026](#bib.bib2)). We
hypothesize that the quality of a model’s moral judgments depends on the
quality of its arguments; therefore, rewarding good argumentation is a
natural way to improve them. Doing so faces three obstacles: subjective
ethical justifications lack rule-based verifiers ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)), monolithic scalar rewards lack resolution for
multi-dimensional argument quality ([Bohnet et al., 2024](#bib.bib7);
[Wachsmuth et al., 2017](#bib.bib58)), and training on model-generated
data erases distributional tails ([Shumailov et al., 2024](#bib.bib55)).

To address these obstacles, we optimize moral argumentation through
reinforcement learning in a self-judged tournament. The policy argues
each dilemma from the perspective of one assigned ethical framework
(e.g., utilitarianism), generating a group of competing arguments. The
policy then judges them pairwise across a multi-dimensional argument
quality taxonomy ([Wachsmuth et al., 2017](#bib.bib58)), yielding the
reward signal. Rao–Kupper preferences ([Rao and Kupper,
1967](#bib.bib49)) convert the comparisons into REINFORCE Leave-One-Out
(RLOO) advantages ([Ahmadian et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)), and masked
thinking restricts the policy gradient to visible answer tokens ([Drori
et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)). Instead of synthetic data, we extract
literature dilemmas from the PG19 corpus ([Rae et al.,
2020](#bib.bib47)) (e.g., _Les Misérables_). Because unverified dilemmas
permit trivial compromises the reward can exploit ([Ouyang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib45)), a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver ([de
Moura and Bjørner, 2008](#bib.bib16)) verifies that the encoded duties
cannot be jointly satisfied.

Rewarding argument quality assumes that better arguments yield better
moral judgment; the competing risk is that optimization selects for how
arguments sound. We therefore track the policy’s linguistic register
during training ([Biber, 1988](#bib.bib6)) and test its moral judgment
on held-out benchmarks. Focusing on the Gemma-4 4B policy, we ask (RQ1,
_mechanism_) what linguistic features the reward selects, and whether
they form a prescriptive register
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"));
(RQ2, _transfer_) how this register transfers to moral judgment and
decision consistency on held-out benchmarks
(§[6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Consistent, yet Pliable under Reframing ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"));
and (RQ3, _ablations_) how dilemma source and masked thinking shape
these effects
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

First, we find that our judge rates argument quality like human
annotators, with model scale mainly reducing presentation flips
(§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Second, the policy adopts a prescriptive register, decisive rather than
dogmatic: answers trade caveats and backward justifications for forward
obligations
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Third, decisiveness and moral judgment diverge on held-out benchmarks:
presentation flips halve, but sycophancy stays flat, framing acceptance
rises, and accuracy falls
(§[6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Consistent, yet Pliable under Reframing ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"));
both ablations replicate it
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Consistency is thus not validity: it can be optimized without improving
the moral judgment it is meant to signal.

## 2 Related Work

Most machine ethics benchmarks frame moral evaluation as discrete label
prediction over short vignettes, letting models exploit surface cues
([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib28); [Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31)). Critics call such closed classification a category
error that flattens value pluralism and ignores non-monotonic
deliberation ([Talat et al., 2022](#bib.bib57); [Hancox-Li and
Blili-Hamelin, 2024](#bib.bib27)). Narrative ethics ([MacIntyre,
2007](#bib.bib40); [Nussbaum, 1992](#bib.bib44)) instead casts moral
judgment as weighing competing duties and virtues against each other
([Bench-Capon, 2003](#bib.bib4); [Rao et al., 2023](#bib.bib48); [Zhou
et al., 2024](#bib.bib64)). While deliberative alignment improves safety
through principles ([Guan et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Jin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32)), moral evaluation requires auditing argumentative
traces rather than isolated decisions ([Neuman et al.,
2025](#bib.bib43)).

Newer benchmarks introduce contextual ambiguity, adversarial fables, and
sycophancy stress-tests ([Scherrer et al., 2023](#bib.bib53); [Marcuzzo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Cheng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib12)), yet on
everyday dilemmas, models disagree with humans and with each other
([Sachdeva and van Nuenen, 2025](#bib.bib52)). While synthetic
generation cheaply scales data diversity ([Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib60)), recursive generation risks distributional collapse
([Shumailov et al., 2024](#bib.bib55)). Canonical literature instead
supplies authentic interpersonal stakes and structural depth ([Nussbaum,
1992](#bib.bib44)), enabling game-theoretic analysis of story structure
([Daskalakis et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)).

Computational Argumentation Quality Assessment evaluates arguments
across logical, rhetorical, and dialectical dimensions ([Wachsmuth et
al., 2017](#bib.bib58); [Stahl et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)). Pairwise
tournament ranking ([Bradley and Terry, 1952](#bib.bib8)) avoids the
rating compression of point-scale grading ([Bohnet et al.,
2024](#bib.bib7)). Policy gradients excel in verifiable domains ([Shao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib54); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)), but
normative reasoning lacks rule-based verifiers, restricting prior
reinforcement learning to keyword heuristics and discrete rules ([An and
Du, 2026](#bib.bib2)). Self-rewarding and self-play methods offer an
alternative ([Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10)), and zero-sum self-play incentivizes reasoning that
transfers beyond games ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)). Yet optimizing
a learned reward invites reward hacking ([Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib21);
[MacDiarmid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)).

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Literature-Grounded Dilemmas

Training dilemmas must force a choice between two duties. We mine such
conflicts from four classical works in the PG19 corpus ([Rae et al.,
2020](#bib.bib47)), using Gemma-4 31B (30.7B parameters) as extractor.
Alongside each dilemma, the extractor formalizes a situational premise
$`P`$ and two competing duty assertions $`D_{1}`$ and $`D_{2}`$ as
Boolean SMT constraints. We verify these assertions using the Z3 solver
([de Moura and Bjørner, 2008](#bib.bib16)) under three formal criteria:
(1) $`P\land D_{1}`$ is satisfiable, (2) $`P\land D_{2}`$ is
satisfiable, and (3) $`P\land D_{1}\land D_{2}`$ is unsatisfiable. Each
duty can thus be fulfilled, but no course of action fulfills both,
leaving no compromise (Appendix
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Z3 Gate Failures ‣ Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Of 185 raw candidates, 156 pass all three criteria (Table
[1](#A1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A.1 Literature Pool ‣ Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"),
Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

To diversify the argumentative positions the policy is trained on, we
pair each verified dilemma with five ethical frameworks as lenses ([Zhou
et al., 2024](#bib.bib64); [Dubey et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)): Kantian
deontology, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, care ethics, and social
contract theory. This expansion produces 780 training prompts that pose
identical narrative premises under contrasting principles.

### 3.2 The Self-Judged Tournament

We initialize the policy from instruction-tuned Gemma-4 E4B ([Gemma
Team, 2026](#bib.bib22)), which has 4.5B effective and 8B total
parameters; we call it 4B. For each training prompt, the policy adopts a
philosophical scholar persona (Appendix
[G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2 Policy Prompt ‣ Appendix G Prompts ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"))
and generates $`G=8`$ completions, separating a chain-of-thought
thinking block from a visible answer. To evaluate argument quality
without score saturation, the policy itself compares them pairwise as
its own judge ([Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)), sharing weights and
updating at each training step ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)). The
judge prompt builds on Wachsmuth’s 15-dimension taxonomy ([Wachsmuth et
al., 2017](#bib.bib58); Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
The judge reasons over all 15 dimensions in its chain of thought but
emits only four pairwise preferences, for _logic_, _rhetoric_,
_dialectic_, and _overall quality_, which keeps decoding short and
parsing robust. The overall preference is the reward; the three
dimension preferences serve as diagnostics
(§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

To counteract position bias ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib63)), we
conduct a full round-robin tournament within each generation group. We
evaluate all $`\binom{8}{2}=28`$ pairs in both presentation orders (56
judgments per prompt) with prefix caching. If the judge prefers a
different completion under reversed order, the outcome is a
_presentation flip_: the preference follows presentation rather than
content. Training scores presentation flips as ties, preserving gradient
signal across evenly matched completions (Table
[4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Training Configuration ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

### 3.3 Tie-Aware Policy Advantage

Because the tournament produces ties, standard Bradley–Terry models
([Bradley and Terry, 1952](#bib.bib8)) are insufficient; we instead
estimate latent argument strengths under the Rao–Kupper formulation
([Rao and Kupper, 1967](#bib.bib49)), introducing an explicit tie
parameter $`\nu>1`$ such that
$`{P(y_{i}\succ y_{j})=e^{s_{i}}/(e^{s_{i}}+\nu e^{s_{j}})}`$. A
symmetric MAP prior regularizes latent strengths against a neutral
baseline, preventing score divergence on undefeated or winless
completions (Table
[4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Training Configuration ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
To counteract verbosity bias ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib63); [Dubois
et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), a within-group length penalty subtracts each
completion’s token-length $`z`$-score (mean $`\mu_{|y|}`$, standard
deviation $`\sigma_{|y|}`$) scaled by coefficient
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}>0`$. Standard GRPO divides advantages by the
group reward standard deviation, which biases updates toward
low-variance prompts ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)). We therefore
retain GRPO’s group sampling and clipped surrogate loss, but compute
policy advantages under REINFORCE Leave-One-Out (RLOO; [Ahmadian et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1)), subtracting the leave-one-out group mean without
variance scaling:

|     |                         |                                                           |        |         |
| --- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ------- | --- | ------------ | --- | ----- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle r_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=s*{i}-\lambda*{\mathrm{len}}\cdot\frac{   | y\_{i} | -\mu\_{ | y   | }}{\sigma\_{ | y   | }},`$ |     | (1) |
|     | $`\displaystyle A_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=r_{i}-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\neq i}r_{j}.`$ |        | (2)     |

Finally, because output-focused rewards can still pressure the chain of
thought ([Korbak et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)), we mask policy gradients on
thinking tokens ([Drori et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)), concentrating
optimization on visible answer tokens. We regularize the full sequence
against the Base checkpoint via token-level KL divergence ($`\beta>0`$;
[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)).

## 4 Experimental Setup

### 4.1 Checkpoints and Baselines

We compare the starting Gemma-4 4B checkpoint (Base) against the policy
trained with GRPO for two epochs (GRPO; Table
[4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Training Configuration ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"))
on the 156 literature dilemmas (Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Gemma-4 31B never enters training; it serves as a reference judge to
test whether judge quality scales with model size
(§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
To determine whether post-training acquires new capabilities or merely
activates latent behaviors, we benchmark Base against leak-free
in-context demonstrations ($`k{=}4{}`$; [Dai et al., 2023](#bib.bib14);
Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E In-Context Baselines and External Judge ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
All evaluations use uniform decoding ($`T{=}0.7`$, top-$`p{=}0.95`$)
with thinking enabled, and we run the benchmarks with vLLM ([Kwon et
al., 2023](#bib.bib34)).

### 4.2 Motivated Ablations

Two ablations each remove one GRPO design choice. First, to test
chain-of-thought monitorability when optimization targets final answers
([Korbak et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Drori et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)),
Unmasked applies policy gradients and length penalties to thinking
tokens as well as visible answers. Second, to test whether narrative
literature drives the learned register, Synthetic trains on dilemmas
generated without literary grounding (Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

### 4.3 Held-Out Benchmarks

To test whether post-training improves moral judgment, we evaluate three
out-of-distribution benchmarks relative to the literature dilemmas.
MoralChoice ([Scherrer et al., 2023](#bib.bib53)) evaluates whether
verdicts survive reversed presentation order, on 587 low-ambiguity and
680 high-ambiguity scenarios. ELEPHANT ([Cheng et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib12)) measures conversational indirectness, framing
acceptance, and moral sycophancy (siding with the narrator) on 1,391
everyday advice posts. MORABLES ([Marcuzzo et al., 2025](#bib.bib41))
probes allegorical moral accuracy by pairing 709 classical fables with
counterfactual rewrites. Presentation flips, moral sycophancy, and
MORABLES accuracy need no judge; the evaluated model scores the other
ELEPHANT metrics, and the 31B judge re-scores them. Presentation flips
measure consistency; moral sycophancy, framing acceptance, and MORABLES
accuracy measure validity: whether a judgment withstands the user’s
premises and matches the reference moral.

### 4.4 Measuring Register Change

To trace stylistic change, we analyze completions across 101 features
spanning layout, syntax, discourse relations, and stance ([Biber,
1988](#bib.bib6); Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Register Features and Assigned Frameworks ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Evaluating 753 paired comparisons between epoch-2 and epoch-1 answers
per group ($`G{=}8`$), we call features _replicated_ if they change
consistently across all three trained runs ($`q<.05`$,
Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control on a dilemma-clustered
bootstrap; [Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995](#bib.bib5)). To isolate the
judge’s influence, we measure _reward attribution_ as the regression
slope of completion advantage $`A_{i}`$ on standardized feature value
within each prompt’s group.

## 5 Judge Validation

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: 4B Base, 4B after GRPO (step 48), and 31B judges on
IBM-ArgQ-30k across the human preference gap $`\Delta`$ (bands: 95%
Wilson CIs). Top: resolved accuracy. Bottom: presentation-flip rate
(dashed), explicit tie rate (dotted), and pair density $`p(\Delta)`$
(histogram).

A self-rewarding policy learns only what its judge rewards. We therefore
evaluate whether the Gemma-4 4B judge, before and after training, and
the 31B reference judge agree with human judgments of argument quality.
We use 15,000 within-topic argument pairs from IBM-ArgQ-30k (1,000 pairs
for each of 15 topics; [Gretz et al., 2020](#bib.bib23)). Crowdsourced
quality scores $`\mathrm{WA}\in[0,1]`$, the weighted share of positive
human ratings, define the human winner, and
$`\Delta=|\mathrm{WA}_{a}-\mathrm{WA}_{b}|`$ measures how strongly
humans prefer it. As in training, the judge evaluates each pair in both
AB and BA presentation orders (30,000 judgments). A pair is _resolved_
if the judge prefers the same argument in both orders. Otherwise the
judge abstains, either with an _explicit tie_ or with a _presentation
flip_. Training scores both as ties
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 The Self-Judged Tournament ‣ 3 Method ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"));
here we keep them apart. We report _resolved accuracy_, the share of
resolved pairs that select the human winner, alongside the _abstention
rate_, the share of all pairs the judge leaves unresolved.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Resolved accuracy and abstention rate of the 4B Base and 31B
judges per aspect and overall on IBM-ArgQ-30k (95% Wilson CIs).
Abstention: share of all pairs, stacked as presentation flips and ties.

Like human annotators ([Gretz et al., 2020](#bib.bib23)), both judges
choose the higher-WA argument least often where human preference is
weakest (Figure
[1](#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"),
top). Resolved accuracy remains near chance on near-ties
($`\Delta\leq 0.25`$; 55.0% at 4B, 57.1% at 31B), but rises in parallel
to 93.3% at 4B and 95.0% at 31B where human preference is strongest
($`\Delta>0.75`$). This alignment extends to expert annotators: on
Dagstuhl-15512 ([Wachsmuth et al., 2017](#bib.bib58)), the 31B judge’s
agreement with each of three experts ($`\tau_{b}=0.47{}`$, 0.45, and
0.45) falls within the inter-expert range (0.428–0.545; Figure
[7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

Resolved accuracy remains comparable across model sizes (78.5% at 4B vs.
80.4% at 31B), but consistency under reordering diverges (Figure
[1](#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"),
bottom). The 31B judge steadily reduces presentation flips, falling from
16.6% on near-ties to 2.6% where human preference is strongest. The 4B
judge starts at twice that rate and declines at a similar pace, from
35.1% to 22.7%, a residual that points to limited capacity rather than
difficult comparisons. Explicit ties are rare at both scales (3.6% at
4B; 0.4% at 31B), so indecision shows almost entirely as presentation
flips. Model size thus primarily improves consistency under reordering
rather than resolved accuracy, lowering the abstention rate from 33.5%
to 10.7%.

Because the judge shares the policy’s weights, training changes it as
well (Figure
[1](#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable"),
purple). On the 6,433 pairs both checkpoints resolve, the 4B judge after
GRPO selects the human winner as often as before (82.2% vs. 82.4%;
difference $`-`$0.2 points, 95% CI \[$`-`$0.5, +0.1\]), but it leaves
47.3% of all pairs unresolved (before: 33.5%), through presentation
flips (38.5%) and explicit ties (8.8%).

Model size also shifts which dimensions the judges leave unresolved
(Figure
[2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")):
the 4B judge abstains most on logic and least on rhetoric, whereas the
31B judge reverses this order. At both scales, the dimension with the
highest abstention rate also reaches the highest resolved accuracy,
which is consistent with abstaining on the harder pairs rather than with
sounder evaluation. The overall reward preference likewise aligns most
often with rhetoric at 4B and with logic at 31B (Table
[6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")
in the appendix). It nevertheless represents all three dimensions and
yields the lowest abstention rate, so we use it as the sole reward.
Section
[7.1](#S7.SS1 "7.1 The Judge Selects the Register ‣ 7 Discussion ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")
tests whether the 4B judge also leans on rhetoric on the policy’s own
answers.

## 6 Policy Results

### 6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register

To answer RQ1, we compare completions across their two visits to the
training dilemmas. The policy learns a register for issuing verdicts
(Figure
[3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")):
completions shift from exploratory analysis toward direct, categorical
pronouncements.

Presentation and syntactic structure simplify in tandem: bullet items
and bold emphasis replace hierarchical headings and numbered lists,
turning structured outlines into direct advice. Sentences shorten,
coordination displaces subordination ($`-`$0.72 SD), and dependency
trees flatten. Sentence length alone does not explain this flattening:
maximum dependency depth falls by $`-`$0.18 SD net of length (95% CI
\[$`-`$0.23, $`-`$0.13\]).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Paired change in replicated register features, epoch 2 vs.
epoch 1 (ratio, log axis; 95% dilemma-clustered bootstrap CIs). Faded:
Unmasked and Synthetic ablations.

Discourse relations reverse direction between training visits: epoch-1
answers justify claims backward using causal connectives (because),
whereas epoch-2 answers derive forward obligations (must; Example 1):

> (1) State Execution and Human Dignity (deontology, GRPO):  
> (1a) Epoch 1, step 5: A thing of dignity, however, holds intrinsic,
> unconditional worth because it is a rational agent capable of giving
> the Moral Law to itself (autonomy).  
> (1b) Epoch 2, step 47: To resolve it, we must move beyond
> sentimentality or utilitarian calculus (the potential societal benefit
> of terrifying the populace) and engage directly with the structure of
> the Categorical Imperative.

Across all prompts, causal and concessive connectives fall (because,
though, even if), while inferential conjuncts rise (thus). Instead of
weighing competing duties against concessions, the policy derives a
binding verdict.

Stance markers change most. Necessity modals (must, should) surge by
1.01 SD in GRPO (Unmasked 0.99, Synthetic 1.02) and by 0.26 SD net of
answer length; time adverbials (+73%) and negation rise too. Possibility
modals (can, may, might) rise in parallel, suggesting that completions
prescribe more without turning dogmatic.

The shift is a register, not an ethical doctrine. Feature identity
accounts for 85% of the variance across the five assigned ethical
frameworks. Frameworks change the size of a shift (at most 15% of the
variance) but rarely its direction: 86% of features keep their sign
under every framework, and only two reverse reliably, both under Kantian
prompts (Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Register Features and Assigned Frameworks ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Kantian vocabulary even declines under Kantian prompts (21.9 to 18.9 per
1,000 words), so training does not commit the policy to a single
philosophical school.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Training reward per within-group SD of replicated features and
the scholar persona ($`x`$) against paired change, epoch 2 vs. epoch 1,
in GRPO ($`y`$, in SD). Shaded quadrants: change in the rewarded
direction. Filled: $`q<.05`$ (BH).

The training reward selects this register directly (Figure
[4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Of the replicated features, 50% have a significant reward association
($`q<.05`$, BH), and 82% of these shift in the rewarded direction.
Across all register features, reward alignment and observed change
correlate strongly ($`\rho=0.61{}`$). The reward favors necessity modals
above all other features (+0.12 per SD). Conversely, the scholar-persona
echo and bullet items spread despite slightly negative reward gradients.

### 6.2 Consistent, yet Pliable under Reframing

For RQ2, we evaluate the policy on the held-out benchmarks (Figure
[5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.2 Consistent, yet Pliable under Reframing ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")):
the register translates into decisiveness, yet moral judgment does not
follow.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Held-out benchmark change, GRPO (step 48) vs. Base (percentage
points; item-paired 95% bootstrap CIs). Crosses: targeted 4-shot ICL vs.
Base (no matched MORABLES run; arrowheads: values past the axis).
Squares: the same GRPO$`-`$Base difference re-scored by a frozen 31B
judge (hollow: CI includes zero). $`\uparrow`$/$`\downarrow`$:
higher/lower is better. ^(‡)Scored by the evaluated model (for ICL, by
Base).

The policy commits firmly under reordering. On high-ambiguity
MoralChoice scenarios, reversing option presentation flips Base’s
verdict in 14.3% of pairs, but only 6.6% in GRPO. This stability does
not come from ignoring moral conflict: the policy recognizes ambiguity
slightly more often than Base (19.1% vs. 16.0%). On ELEPHANT,
conversational indirectness falls from 25.5% to 6.2%: hedged advice
gives way to direct verdicts, echoing the training register
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

Moral judgment does not improve in parallel. On ELEPHANT, moral
sycophancy remains flat (45.3% in Base vs. 44.0% in GRPO): the policy
sides with the narrator from both perspectives rather than forming an
independent moral judgment. Susceptibility to the user’s framing
increases, with framing acceptance rising from 5.2% to 7.5%. A frozen
31B judge confirms both self-scored shifts on the same completions:
indirectness falls ($`-`$10.6 points, 95% CI \[$`-`$12.3, $`-`$8.9\])
and framing acceptance rises (+4.3 points, 95% CI \[+1.5, +7.0\];
squares in Figure
[5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.2 Consistent, yet Pliable under Reframing ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
although the two judges flag framing at very different rates (Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E In-Context Baselines and External Judge ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
On MORABLES fables, the only benchmark with unambiguous normative
correctness, five-way accuracy drops from 56.5% to 53.4% ($`-`$3.1
points, 95% CI \[$`-`$4.8, $`-`$1.5\]).

Four targeted demonstrations reach comparable consistency under
reordering without training (ICL-targeted; Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E In-Context Baselines and External Judge ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Base then shows fewer presentation flips than GRPO (2.1%), near-zero
indirectness (0.1%), and lower moral sycophancy (26.8%). However,
demonstrations call 32 of the 587 low-ambiguity consensus scenarios
irresolvable (Base: 5; GRPO: 3) and raise framing acceptance to 29.0% of
posts. While consistency under reordering improves under arbitrary
demonstrations (random: 4.3%), lowering sycophancy requires curated
targets (random: 48.8%; Table
[8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix E In-Context Baselines and External Judge ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

### 6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations

RQ3 asks whether this divergence depends on loss masking or narrative
grounding (Figure
[6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
With one seed per run, we attribute an effect to a factor only if one
ablation diverges from GRPO and the other does not. The divergence
itself recurs in all three runs. Both ablations keep GRPO’s consistency
under reordering, changing the presentation-flip rate by only +0.7
points in Unmasked (95% CI \[$`-`$1.3, +2.8\]) and +1.0 in Synthetic
(\[$`-`$0.9, +3.1\]), yet both are more sycophantic than GRPO (+3.7
points, 95% CI \[+1.2, +5.9\]; +4.6, \[+2.6, +6.9\]).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: Held-out benchmark change, Unmasked and Synthetic vs. GRPO
(percentage points; item-paired 95% bootstrap CIs; rows as in Figure
[5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.2 Consistent, yet Pliable under Reframing ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Squares: the same Unmasked$`-`$GRPO difference re-scored by a frozen 31B
judge (Synthetic not re-scored). Hollow: CI includes zero.

Masking decides where the policy spends its words. The training reward
favors longer thinking in all runs (+0.19 per SD in GRPO, +0.09 in
Unmasked; Figure
[4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
but masking hides thinking tokens from the policy gradient. GRPO’s
thinking shrinks from 392 to 265 words while its answers grow from 780
to 1,078 (Figure
[9](#A6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Unmasked follows the reward instead: its thinking grows (+47%) more than
its answers (+17%), whose growth stalls in epoch 2 (9% of the total, vs.
30% in GRPO). Masking also reduces the lexical overlap between thinking
and answers ($`-`$35%; Unmasked: +4%).

This reallocation trades one benchmark against another. On MORABLES
fables, Unmasked recovers part of GRPO’s accuracy loss (+2.1 points over
GRPO, 95% CI \[+0.7, +3.6\]) without thinking longer (387.6 vs. 400.5
words; Figure
[10](#A6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")
in Appendix
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
but stays below Base. On ELEPHANT, it thinks longer than GRPO (461.8 vs.
343.2 words) and accepts the user’s framing more often (+5.8 points, 95%
CI \[+3.7, +7.8\]; 31B judge: +6.6, \[+3.8, +9.3\]). Its self-scored
gain in directness ($`-`$3.2 points, 95% CI \[$`-`$4.6, $`-`$1.7\]) does
not survive the 31B judge, under which both runs are already near zero.

The ablations differ in how much register they carry. Of the features
GRPO shifts significantly ($`q<.05`$), Synthetic replicates 69% at
nearly full strength (0.92 median magnitude). Unmasked replicates a
similar share (71%) but at only 0.71 of GRPO’s magnitude. Literature
thus barely shapes the register, whereas unmasking dilutes it.

## 7 Discussion

The goal of self-improvement for machine ethics is normative competence,
not persuasiveness ([Talat et al., 2022](#bib.bib57); [Hancox-Li and
Blili-Hamelin, 2024](#bib.bib27); [Sachdeva and van Nuenen,
2025](#bib.bib52)). Our 4B policy learns a prescriptive register that
transfers as decisiveness rather than as better judgment.

### 7.1 The Judge Selects the Register

Optimizing against an automated judge invites Goodhart’s law: a policy
can satisfy the judge through whatever correlates with its preference
([Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib63)). The
change we observe is not a set of disparate surface tricks but one
register that recurs under every assigned framework
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

Judge validation raised a specific risk: on human-written arguments, the
4B judge’s overall preference agreed most often with its rhetoric
preference, its weakest predictor of human preference
(§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
On the policy’s own completions, however, diagnostic logging across 144
prompt groups shows that the overall reward follows dialectic (mean
Spearman $`\rho=0.94{}`$), then logic (0.68), and rhetoric least (0.53).
Rhetoric still leaves a trace: it specifically favors shallower
dependency trees ($`-`$0.09 SD per SD of maximum depth, 95% CI
\[$`-`$0.16, $`-`$0.03\]). Outcome accuracy on human arguments therefore
does not reveal which aspect drives the judge on the policy’s
distribution ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib59)); only the policy’s own
rollouts do.

The answers grow although the training reward does not favor length. The
raw judge favors longer answers within each group (+0.30 SD of advantage
per SD of answer length, 95% CI \[+0.24, +0.37\]), but the leave-one-out
length penalty flattens this preference ($`-`$0.04 SD). Answers lengthen
nonetheless, because within-group normalization cannot penalize drift
that all completions in a group share. The register itself is one source
of such drift: in the policy’s output, the rewarded stance markers
co-occur with longer answers, and masking leaves the visible answer as
the only channel for optimization pressure. GRPO’s response-level loss
normalization may also favor longer completions ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38)). Either way, the growth is a byproduct of learning
the register under masking, not length gaming against a slipping
penalty.

### 7.2 Decisive but Pliable

The policy commits more often and more stably, but it commits within the
frame the user supplies. Consistency under reordering and framing
acceptance rise in GRPO, neither ablation reverses them, and sycophancy
falls in no run. This consistency is specific to the rewarded role: the
same weights that halve presentation flips on MoralChoice flip more
often as a pairwise judge on IBM-ArgQ (29.9% before training, 38.5%
after;
§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
One account links decisiveness and pliability: a policy rewarded for
verdicts learns to reach one, and the cheapest premise for a verdict is
the one in the prompt. Normative ethics offers no rule-based verifier
that would penalize a false premise ([Creswell and Shanahan,
2022](#bib.bib13); [Jacovi et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)). In-context
demonstrations fit the same account: they make Base the most direct and
most consistent model under reordering we test, and they raise framing
acceptance more than any training run does. The rise in framing
acceptance is not an artifact of self-scoring: a frozen 31B judge
registers it in GRPO and, more strongly, in Unmasked. Persistent
sycophancy is not harmless: even one sycophantic exchange makes users
less willing to repair conflicts ([Cheng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)).

### 7.3 Masking Is a Lever with a Price

Masking determines which channel absorbs policy optimization
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Without masking, the policy gradient spreads across the full sequence
instead of concentrating on the answer; under per-token loss
normalization, this dilution may explain why Unmasked acquires the
register more weakly and degrades less on MORABLES fables.

This choice creates a dilemma for chain-of-thought monitorability
([Korbak et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)). No policy gradient reaches thinking
tokens, yet the answer repeats less of the thinking
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
consistent with feedback spillover through shared weights ([Drori et
al., 2026](#bib.bib17)). Lexical overlap is not faithfulness ([Jacovi et
al., 2024](#bib.bib30)), but masking risks divorcing the stated
justification from the verdict.

Exposing thinking to optimization does not resolve the policy’s
pliability either. Unmasked thinks longer than GRPO on ELEPHANT and
accepts the user’s framing more often, yet longer traces go with framing
acceptance only within GRPO (Table
[9](#A6.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")
in Appendix
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Without an external verifier, longer deliberation does not make the
policy judge the user’s premises independently.

### 7.4 What Narrative Grounding Changes

Grounding training dilemmas in classical literature does not induce the
prescriptive register: Synthetic replicates most of it at nearly full
strength
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
so the register reflects the automated judge’s preferences rather than
the stylistic richness of nineteenth-century texts. Narrative grounding
reliably influences only directness: synthetic training makes answers
+5.6 points more indirect (95% CI \[+3.7, +7.6\]). Verified literary
conflicts ensure genuine moral tension during training, but pairwise
reinforcement learning distills a way of arguing rather than sound moral
deliberation.

## 8 Conclusion

We investigated whether rewarding argument quality in a self-judged
tournament improves moral judgment. We trained a Gemma-4 4B policy with
masked thinking on literature dilemmas verified with an SMT solver. Our
judge rates argument quality like human annotators, and reinforcement
learning instills a prescriptive register: answers trade caveats and
backward justifications for forward obligations across every assigned
ethical framework. On held-out benchmarks, this register makes the
policy decisive, halving presentation flips on ambiguous MoralChoice
scenarios and making its ELEPHANT replies more direct.

Decisive verdicts, however, do not yield more valid moral judgments: on
ELEPHANT posts, moral sycophancy remains flat while framing acceptance
rises; on MORABLES fables, allegorical accuracy falls. Both ablations
match the reordering gains but show a weaker register shift and higher
moral sycophancy. Training on synthetic dilemmas preserves most of the
register, so it comes from the reward rather than the literary source.
Unmasking the thinking weakens the register most and reduces the
MORABLES drop, but increases framing acceptance. Consistency under
reordering, a common proxy for moral validity, can thus be optimized
without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal. Machine
ethics research should therefore evaluate consistency and validity
separately.

## Limitations

Our reward comes from a single design: the policy judges its own
completions with shared weights. Because no run trains against a fixed
judge such as the 31B model, we cannot tell whether the register arises
from self-judgment or from pairwise argument-quality rewards in general.
Shared weights may also lead the judge to favor familiar completions, a
form of self-preference bias ([Panickssery et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)).
We have also not tested the prediction of
§[7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Decisive but Pliable ‣ 7 Discussion ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")
that framing acceptance rises with decisiveness during training.

Our judges are validated only on human-written arguments
(§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
not on policy completions, and no human evaluates the policy’s
arguments. The central divergence therefore rests on three metrics that
need no judge: presentation flips, moral sycophancy, and MORABLES
accuracy. The evaluated model and a frozen Gemma-4 31B judge from the
same model family score the remaining ELEPHANT metrics, and neither is
validated against human annotations. The two judges agree on the
direction of change but only weakly on individual items (Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E In-Context Baselines and External Judge ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
so we interpret direction rather than level.

Our findings come from a narrow experimental scope. We train one policy
scale, Gemma-4 4B, always with thinking enabled, and each configuration
only once. The divergence recurs in all three runs
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
but our confidence intervals reflect variation across dilemmas and
benchmark items, not across training runs. All dilemmas are in English,
and the literature dilemmas come from four nineteenth-century Western
novels.

Formal verification covers the conflict, not its resolution. Z3 checks
the extractor’s Boolean encoding of each dilemma, not the narrative
itself, and the encoding states every duty as a hard constraint
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Literature-Grounded Dilemmas ‣ 3 Method ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
The check confirms that no action fulfills both duties, but the encoding
cannot express that one duty outweighs the other. Many dilemmas turn on
such an ordering ([Bench-Capon, 2003](#bib.bib4)), for example whether
preventing serious harm outweighs keeping a promise. Resolving a dilemma
is thus left to the judge, which no formal check constrains. Weighted
encodings, such as soft constraints in MaxSMT, could make these
orderings explicit.

## Ethical Considerations

The main risk of this work follows from its main finding. Rewarding
argument quality produced a model that commits to verdicts more readily
and more stably. The same model accepts the user’s framing more often,
and its moral judgment does not improve: MORABLES accuracy falls.
Deployed as a moral advisor, such a model would lend confident language
to whatever premises a user brings, and sycophantic advice already
lowers users’ willingness to repair conflicts ([Cheng et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib11)). Because the policy becomes more consistent under
reordering, consistency checks would hide this risk. Decisiveness and
consistency are therefore insufficient evidence of valid moral judgment.
The same reward also teaches the policy to argue any assigned framework
in one confident register
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Reward Selects a Prescriptive Register ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
so the method could produce persuasive rationalizations for a
predetermined verdict. We do not release the trained models.

We take no position on which ethical framework is correct. The five
frameworks serve as assigned lenses, and the policy’s verdicts are not
moral ground truth. The benchmarks carry their own normative
assumptions: ELEPHANT counts accepting the user’s framing as a failure,
and MORABLES scores each fable against a single reference moral. All
five frameworks come from the Western philosophical tradition, which
leaves non-Western and communal ethics unrepresented ([Romberg et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)). The source novels also reflect the views of their
period on class, gender, and religion, and the extracted dilemmas may
carry these views.

We collected no new data from human subjects. The training texts are
public-domain books from PG19, and all models, benchmarks, and datasets
are used in accordance with their licenses and terms of use. ELEPHANT
contains posts written by online users; we use the released data as
provided and make no attempt to identify their authors. We used AI
assistants for writing and coding; the authors reviewed all output and
take full responsibility for the content.

## Appendix A Dilemma Data

### A.1 Literature Pool

The literature pool (LitPool) is drawn from four PG19 novels by Hugo,
Austen, Melville, and Dostoevsky. _Les Misérables_ supplies the largest
share of the extracted dilemmas, and compassion is the most frequent
competing value (Table
[1](#A1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A.1 Literature Pool ‣ Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
The extraction prompt is shown in Appendix
[G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Dilemma Extraction Prompt ‣ Appendix G Prompts ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable").

| Author     | Source Work                    | Extracted |
| ---------- | ------------------------------ | --------- |
| Hugo       | _Les Misérables_ (#135)        | 88        |
| Austen     | _Pride and Prejudice_ (#1342)  | 39        |
| Melville   | _Moby-Dick_ (#2701)            | 33        |
| Dostoevsky | _Crime and Punishment_ (#2554) | 25        |
| Total      |                                | 185       |

| Value-concept     | Count | % of pool |
| ----------------- | ----- | --------- |
| compassion        | 41    | 22.2%     |
| honesty           | 19    | 10.3%     |
| integrity         | 18    | 9.7%      |
| self preservation | 18    | 9.7%      |
| professional duty | 15    | 8.1%      |
| moral discipline  | 14    | 7.6%      |
| autonomy          | 14    | 7.6%      |
| familial duty     | 11    | 5.9%      |
| legal obedience   | 9     | 4.9%      |
| pragmatism        | 7     | 3.8%      |

Table 1: Curriculum dilemma pool (LitPool). Top: dilemmas extracted per
PG19 source work (Gutenberg ID). Bottom: most frequent competing
value-concepts among the 185 extracted dilemmas, of which 156 pass the
Z3 gate and are trained on.

### A.2 Z3 Gate Failures

Most generated synthetic dilemmas pass the Z3 gate (77.7%; Table
[2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ A.2 Z3 Gate Failures ‣ Appendix A Dilemma Data ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
Most of the rest are not genuine dilemmas: their duties can be satisfied
together ($`Z{=}1`$, 15.4%). The few degenerate encodings ($`Z{=}0`$)
are mostly over-constrained: the premise fixes a fact that one duty then
negates, so that duty alone is unsatisfiable. The Synthetic run trains
on the gate passes of this batch and of a second batch, with exact
duplicates removed.

|                                  |             |
| -------------------------------- | ----------- |

## Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation

The judge prompt follows the taxonomy of [Wachsmuth et al.
(2017)](#bib.bib58): three aspects, each with an aspect-level dimension
and its sub-dimensions, plus overall quality (Table
[5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
The judge reasons through all 15 dimensions in its thinking and then
emits four verdicts, one per aspect and one for overall quality. Only
the overall verdict enters the reward.

|                      |                                                                                     |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Dimension            | Question in the judge prompt                                                        |
| Logic                |                                                                                     |
| Cogency              | Are the premises acceptable, relevant to the conclusion, and sufficient to draw it? |
| Local acceptability  | Are the premises rationally worthy of belief?                                       |
| Local relevance      | Do the premises actually bear on the conclusion?                                    |
| Local sufficiency    | Do the premises together give enough support?                                       |
| Rhetoric             |                                                                                     |
| Effectiveness        | Does the argument persuade the target audience of the stance?                       |
| Credibility          | Does it make the author worthy of credence (ethos)?                                 |
| Emotional appeal     | Does it make a successful emotional appeal (pathos)?                                |
| Clarity              | Does it use correct, widely unambiguous, on-topic language?                         |
| Appropriateness      | Are the language and tone proportional to the issue?                                |
| Arrangement          | Are the issue, arguments, and conclusion in a proper order?                         |
| Dialectic            |                                                                                     |
| Reasonableness       | Does it help resolve the issue acceptably and sufficiently?                         |
| Global acceptability | Would the audience accept the arguments and framing?                                |
| Global relevance     | Does it contribute to resolving the issue at hand?                                  |
| Global sufficiency   | Does it rebut anticipatable counter-arguments?                                      |
| Overall quality      | A holistic judgment of overall argument quality, considering all dimensions above.  |

Table 5: The 15 argument-quality dimensions of [Wachsmuth et al.
(2017)](#bib.bib58) as phrased in the judge prompt (Appendix
[G.3](#A7.SS3 "G.3 Pairwise Judge Prompt ‣ Appendix G Prompts ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")),
grouped by aspect; sub-dimensions are indented under their aspect. The
judge reasons over all 15 but emits only four verdicts: logic, rhetoric,
dialectic, and overall quality.

The agreement with experts in
§[5](#S5 "5 Judge Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")
holds for every dimension: the 31B judge’s agreement with each expert
lies within or above the range of agreement between experts (Figure
[7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
The aspect verdicts rarely contradict the reward. Nearly all mismatches
are presentation flips or ties: an aspect selects the other argument on
at most 1.2% of the pairs with a decisive overall verdict (Table
[6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Judge Rubric and Validation ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length

Loss masking moves length out of thinking and into the answer. Over
training, GRPO’s thinking contracts while its answers expand, whereas
Unmasked lengthens both, its thinking most (Figure
[9](#A6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable");
§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 The Divergence Survives Both Ablations ‣ 6 Policy Results ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).
On held-out benchmarks, Unmasked thinks longest on ELEPHANT but less
than GRPO on MORABLES (Figure
[10](#A6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix F Thinking and Answer Length ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

## Appendix G Prompts

The three prompts below are exported verbatim from the code that ran the
experiments; braces mark template fields.

### G.1 Dilemma Extraction Prompt

Gemma-4 31B receives this prompt once per text chunk. It extracts the
dilemmas in the chunk and encodes each as SMT constraints for the Z3
gate
(§[3](#S3 "3 Method ‣ Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable")).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are an expert moral philosopher AND a formal verification
specialist. Your task has two parts performed together for each dilemma:

1. \*\*Extract\*\* all significant ethical dilemmas from the text chunk
   below.

2. \*\*Formalize\*\* the competing moral duties of each dilemma into Z3
   SMT-LIB format strings.

\## SMT-LIB Formalization Rules

- \`smt_premise\`: Use \`declare-const\` to declare boolean variables
  representing the key narrative constraints and moral facts. Then use
  \`assert\` to encode the situational context.

- \`smt_duty_a\`: One or more \`assert\` statements encoding the
  obligation to fulfill the FIRST competing value.

- \`smt_duty_b\`: One or more \`assert\` statements encoding the
  obligation to fulfill the SECOND competing value.

- The duties SHOULD be mutually exclusive when possible --- this is what
  makes the situation a genuine moral dilemma. Use complementary
  assertions (e.g., \`(assert X)\` vs \`(assert (not X))\`) when the
  values logically conflict.

\## Output Format

Respond exclusively with a valid JSON array of objects. Each object MUST
contain the following keys in EXACTLY this order:

1. "id": a unique short identifier string (e.g., "theft_for_survival")

2. "title": a concise descriptive name for the dilemma

3. "context": a summary of the narrative situation (3-5 sentences)

4. "z3_evaluation": an object with exactly three keys:

- "smt_premise": Z3 SMT-LIB string declaring narrative context as
  logical constraints

- "smt_duty_a": Z3 SMT-LIB string asserting fulfillment of the first
  competing value

- "smt_duty_b": Z3 SMT-LIB string asserting fulfillment of the second
  competing value

5. "dilemma": the core moral question phrased as a question

6. "competing_values": a list of exactly two string values in tension
   (e.g., \["duty", "compassion"\])

7. "context_passage": a key verbatim passage or quote from the text
   capturing the dilemma

\## Example

\[

{

"id": "theft_for_survival",

"title": "Stealing Bread to Feed a Starving Child",

"context": "A man's sister's child is starving. He has no money and no
legal means to obtain food. He breaks a bakery window and steals a loaf
of bread. He is caught and faces imprisonment.",

"z3_evaluation": {

"smt_premise": "(declare-const child_starving Bool)\\n(declare-const
has_legal_means Bool)\\n(declare-const bread_stolen Bool)\\n(assert
child_starving)\\n(assert (not has_legal_means))\\n(assert
bread_stolen)",

"smt_duty_a": "(assert (=\> child_starving bread_stolen))",

"smt_duty_b": "(assert (not bread_stolen))"

},

"dilemma": "Is it morally justified to steal bread to prevent a child
from starving?",

"competing_values": \["compassion", "legal_obedience"\],

"context_passage": "He broke a pane of glass, thrust his arm through,
and seized a loaf of bread."

}

\]

Do not include markdown backticks, conversational wrappers, or any text
outside the JSON array.

\## Text Chunk

{chunk}

### G.2 Policy Prompt

Each training prompt pairs one dilemma with one assigned framework.
Braces mark the fields of the extracted dilemma and the framework label
(Kantian, Utilitarian, Virtue Ethics, Care Ethics, and Social Contract).
The key passage is omitted when a dilemma has none, and the chat
template enables thinking mode.

#### System Prompt

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,WW91IGFyZSBhIHNjaG9sYXIgb2YgbW9yYWwgcGhpbG9zb3BoeSBzcGVjaWFsaXppbmcgaW4ge2ZyYW1ld29ya30uIEFuYWx5emUgZXRoaWNhbCBkaWxlbW1hcyB3aXRoIHJpZ29yb3VzIHBoaWxvc29waGljYWwgcmVhc29uaW5nIGdyb3VuZGVkIGluIHtmcmFtZXdvcmt9Lg==)

You are a scholar of moral philosophy specializing in {framework}.
Analyze ethical dilemmas with rigorous philosophical reasoning grounded
in {framework}.

#### User Prompt Template

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\## Ethical Dilemma: {dilemma_title}

\### Context

{context}

\### Key Passage

"{context_passage}"

\### Central Question

{ethical_question}

\### Competing Moral Values

{competing_values}

\### Task

Analyze and resolve this ethical dilemma strictly through the framework
of \*\*{framework}\*\*.

Ground your reasoning deeply in the core principles of {framework},
address the central moral tensions, and provide a clear, principled, and
justified recommendation on what course of action should be taken.

### G.3 Pairwise Judge Prompt

The judge receives the system prompt and one user prompt per ordered
pair of completions.

#### System Prompt

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are an expert pairwise argument-quality judge for ethical
argumentation. You will be given a moral dilemma, the question at stake,
and two competing argumentations (Argument A and Argument B). Your job
is to decide which argument demonstrates superior reasoning.

Reason step by step THROUGH ALL fifteen Wachsmuth argument-quality
dimensions, grouped by their three aspect tiers. Weigh both arguments on
each dimension before forming your tier-level and overall judgments. Do
NOT be influenced by argument length or writing style beyond what each
dimension itself requires.

\### Tier 1 --- Logic (cogency)

- cogency: Are the premises acceptable, relevant to the conclusion, and
  sufficient to draw it?

- local_acceptability: Are the premises rationally worthy of belief?

- local_relevance: Do the premises actually bear on the conclusion?

- local_sufficiency: Do the premises together give enough support?

\### Tier 2 --- Rhetoric (effectiveness)

- effectiveness: Does the argument persuade the target audience of the
  stance?

- credibility: Does it make the author worthy of credence (ethos)?

- emotional_appeal: Does it make a successful emotional appeal
  (pathos)?

- clarity: Does it use correct, widely unambiguous, on-topic language?

- appropriateness: Are the language and tone proportional to the issue?

- arrangement: Are the issue, arguments, and conclusion in a proper
  order?

\### Tier 3 --- Dialectic (reasonableness)

- reasonableness: Does it help resolve the issue acceptably and
  sufficiently?

- global_acceptability: Would the audience accept the arguments and
  framing?

- global_relevance: Does it contribute to resolving the issue at hand?

- global_sufficiency: Does it rebut anticipatable counter-arguments?

\### Overall

- overall_quality: A holistic judgment of overall argument quality,
  considering all dimensions above.

After reasoning through the dimensions, collapse your assessment into
exactly FOUR verdicts --- one per aspect tier plus the holistic overall:

- "logic": the winner on the Logic tier (Tier 1).

- "rhetoric": the winner on the Rhetoric tier (Tier 2).

- "dialectic": the winner on the Dialectic tier (Tier 3).

- "overall_quality": the holistic winner.

Each verdict MUST be exactly "A" (Argument A is stronger), "B" (Argument
B is stronger), or "tie". Prefer choosing "A" or "B" when any meaningful
difference exists; reserve "tie" for genuine parity.

\### Output Format

After your reasoning, respond with a SINGLE valid JSON object containing
EXACTLY these four keys and nothing else. Do NOT output markdown code
blocks, headers, or any keys other than these four (no justification, no
confidence).

{

"logic": "A" \| "B" \| "tie",

"rhetoric": "A" \| "B" \| "tie",

"dialectic": "A" \| "B" \| "tie",

"overall_quality": "A" \| "B" \| "tie"

}

#### User Prompt Template

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\### Ethical Dilemma

{context}

\### Moral Question

{question}

\### Argument A

{argument_a}

\### Argument B

{argument_b}

\### Your Task

Reason through all fifteen dimensions grouped by tier, then respond with
ONLY the four-field JSON verdict object described above. No markdown, no
commentary.
